prompt: Match each clock of a streamed call to what it decides.

pairs.right: how long the screen stays empty
how long a long answer takes once started
how long a worker and a connection are held

right_distractors: how many tokens the prompt had

prompt: In stream.py's run, how many milliseconds passed before the first piece arrived?
Why does recording the time to first token need a streamed call?

choices.text: Non-streamed calls carry no usage
choices.why: They do carry usage; it is the timing they lose.

choices.text: OpenTelemetry keeps events on streamed spans and drops them on others, so there would be no first-token event
choices.why: Any span can carry events.

choices.text: Without streaming, the first and last tokens arrive together
choices.why: Right. The client cannot see when the provider produced the first one.

choices.text: Providers charge less for streaming
choices.why: Price does not depend on streaming.

prompt: A team shortens its prompt by half and the answers stay the same length. Which clock moves most?

choices.text: Time to first token
choices.why: Right. The first token waits for the prompt to be read; the rest does not.

choices.text: Time per output token
choices.why: It is a property of the model and the provider's load, not of the prompt.

choices.text: The clocks stay as they were, because the prompt is read in parallel with the reply being written out
choices.why: The prompt is read before the first token, and that is what the first clock measures.

choices.text: The number of output tokens
choices.why: The answers stayed the same length, as the question says.

prompt: The week's first-token mean was 353 ms, median 290, p99 4,257. Why is the mean a poor summary?

choices.text: It was computed on too few calls
choices.why: 1,108 calls is plenty; the problem is the shape.

choices.text: Means cannot be computed on milliseconds
choices.why: They can; it is just the wrong summary for a tail.

choices.text: It includes the failed calls
choices.why: latency.py excludes failed calls.

choices.text: It describes nobody
choices.why: Right: too high for the typical call, far too low for the slow one. A tight body and a long tail are two populations a mean blends.

prompt: Why is a p99 call not a rare customer's problem?

choices.text: Because p99 is defined over customers, not calls
choices.why: latency.py computes it over calls.

choices.text: Because a session holds many calls, so many sessions meet one
choices.why: Right. Ten calls give about one chance in ten of at least one p99.

choices.text: Because the slow calls are all from one user
choices.why: The cold starts fall at random, on anybody.

choices.text: Because p99 is the same as the median under load
choices.why: Here it was nearly fifteen times the median.

prompt: What was the median time per output token after the first, in the week's model calls?
Over the week, what did the length of a whole model call follow most closely?

choices.text: The number of output tokens
choices.why: Right. From under 20 to over 80 tokens, the median went from 555 to 2,498 ms.

choices.text: The number of input tokens
choices.why: Input moved the first token by about a tenth of a second across all groups.

choices.text: The hour of the day
choices.why: labobs' timing does not depend on the hour.

choices.text: The feature that made the request
choices.why: Only through how long each feature's answers are.

prompt: Sixteen calls waited over 3 s for a first token, in every input-size group. What does that suggest?

choices.text: Long prompts cause cold starts
choices.why: They appeared at every prompt size, short ones included.

choices.text: The output was very long in those calls
choices.why: The first token comes before any output exists.

choices.text: A bug in drivers.py that grouped them wrongly
choices.why: The grouping is by the span's own token count; the 16 are counted separately anyway.

choices.text: A cause outside the request
choices.why: Right. Slowness that ignores size points at the provider, the network or a queue.

prompt: Match each goal to the lever this lesson pairs with it.
With 30% of attempts refused, two of ten attempts failed and none of ten requests did. Why?

choices.text: The failures were in the embedding, which does not count
choices.why: They were in chat spans.

choices.text: Each failure was retried, and the retry worked
choices.why: Right. The attempt error rate is the provider's health; the request rate is the customer's.

choices.text: errors.py ignores failures
choices.why: It counted two.

choices.text: Refusals are not errors
choices.why: A 503 is an error on the span.

prompt: The attempt error rate rises and the request error rate stays flat. What is the lesson's reading?

choices.text: An incident: page somebody now
choices.why: That is for both rising together.

choices.text: Nothing to see, since no customer was affected
choices.why: The retries are being spent, and they run out.

choices.text: A warning: the retries are absorbing a provider problem
choices.why: Right. It is the time to look, before they run out.

choices.text: A bug in the retry loop
choices.why: The loop is working exactly as intended when this happens.

prompt: With the SDK's own retries, the trace showed one 1,835 ms span and no error. What did labobs' log show?

choices.text: One request that took 1,835 ms
choices.why: There were three requests.

choices.text: Three successes
choices.why: Requests 2362 and 2363 were refused.

choices.text: Two refusals with 503 and then a success
choices.why: Right. The SDK hid both failures inside one successful span.

choices.text: Nothing, because the SDK retries locally
choices.why: Every retry is a new request to the provider.

prompt: Besides retrying in your own code, how can a team keep the SDK's retries and still see each attempt?

choices.text: Instrument underneath, at the HTTP level
choices.why: Right. Each request the SDK sends becomes its own span.

choices.text: Raise max_retries so that failures become rarer than they were before
choices.why: More retries hide more failures.

choices.text: Lower the timeout until the retries stop happening
choices.why: A timeout does not reveal a refusal; it adds another kind of failure.

choices.text: Read the response headers for a retry count
choices.why: The final response does not say how many attempts preceded it.

prompt: How does the assistant tell a stream that was cut from one that finished?

choices.text: The reply is shorter than usual
choices.why: Short replies are normal; length proves nothing.

choices.text: The HTTP status is 500
choices.why: The stream began with 200; the status was sent before any text.

choices.text: The citations are missing
choices.why: A finished reply can lack citations too.

choices.text: No finish reason ever arrived
choices.why: Right. A finished stream ends with one; a dropped one does not.

prompt: A streamed reply is shown on screen as it arrives, gets cut, and is retried. What does the customer see if the screen was not built for it?

choices.text: Nothing different from a slow answer
choices.why: That is true only when the reply is shown complete.

choices.text: The beginning, then the text restarting or doubled
choices.why: Right. A retry of a streamed reply is a visible stutter.

choices.text: An error page with the trace id
choices.why: The retry succeeded; no error reached the screen.

choices.text: Only the second attempt
choices.why: The first six pieces were already on screen.

prompt: The assistant records how far a cut stream got in the attribute app.partial____.
Why is a 1 s timeout on the whole call a bad choice for this assistant?

choices.text: It is longer than the SDK default
choices.why: The default is ten minutes.

choices.text: It never fires
choices.why: It would fire constantly.

choices.text: It cuts long answers too
choices.why: Right. More than half the week took over a second because it had more to say.

choices.text: Timeouts cannot be set on streams
choices.why: They can, as a limit on each read.

prompt: timeout.py's two-second timeout fired on a call that was about to take four. What does the SDK's timeout actually bound?

choices.text: The whole call from start to finish
choices.why: A long stream with no long gap would not trip it.

choices.text: The number of retries
choices.why: That is max_retries, a separate setting.

choices.text: The provider's own processing time, reported back
choices.why: The client cannot see the provider's processing time; it sees only bytes arriving or not.

choices.text: The connection and each read: for a stream, the first piece and the gaps
choices.why: Right. It is the HTTP client's timeout, not a limit on the whole call.

prompt: What is the OpenAI SDK's default timeout, in minutes?
Put the events of the cut-stream trace in the order they happened.
items: the first attempt delivers six pieces
the stream ends with no finish reason
the assistant waits half a second
the second attempt delivers the whole reply

prompt: Which of these belong on a model-call span for latency work? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: The time to the first token
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The output token count
choices.why: Right: time follows it.

choices.text: The input token count
choices.why: Right: the first token follows it.

choices.text: The mean latency of the week
choices.why: A span is one call; a week's summary is computed from many spans.

prompt: Lesson 3 found the input was most of the cost. What does lesson 4 find the output is most of?

choices.text: The time
choices.why: Right. Every output token adds its 25 ms or so.

choices.text: The cost as well, once the price of output is counted properly
choices.why: Input stayed most of the cost even at four times cheaper per token.

choices.text: The failures, since long outputs are cut more often
choices.why: No such pattern was measured here.

choices.text: The tokens sent to the embedding model
choices.why: The embedding reads the question, not the output.

prompt: Which error rate describes what the customers experienced?

choices.text: The attempt error rate
choices.why: That one is the provider's health; retries can hide it from customers.

choices.text: The request error rate
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The rate of cold starts in the week, as labobs' rules set it
choices.why: Cold starts are slow, not failed.

choices.text: The share of refusals by the floor
choices.why: A refusal is an answer, not an error.
